content.title: About
content.content: Biscuit is a light baked product made from eggs, sugar, flour and a small amount of fat. The batter is whisked into an airy foam and then baked at a low temperature, giving the biscuit a porous structure and a gentle flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Biscuit originated in Europe in the 19th century as a yeast‑free light cake.
Traditional biscuit is often used as a base for layered cakes because it absorbs syrups well.
In Russia, “biscuit layers” are a popular component of multi‑layered desserts.
Biscuit can be made sweet or slightly savory depending on added ingredients.
Sometimes starch replaces part of the wheat flour to achieve an even lighter texture.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Biscuit usually contains only a small amount of butter, making it less caloric than many other baked goods.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Biscuit provides a quick source of energy thanks to its carbohydrate content.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs in the recipe add a modest amount of complete protein.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The porous crumb aids digestion, especially in light‑diet regimes.

items.title: Fortification potential
items.content: Vitamins, minerals or protein powders can be incorporated into the batter, making the biscuit more nutritious.

items.title: Egg or gluten allergy
items.content: Biscuit contains eggs and wheat, which may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because of its sugar and simple carbohydrate content, biscuit can raise blood glucose quickly.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain and dental caries.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Biscuit loses freshness rapidly and can become dry or moldy if not stored properly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Biscuit is used as a cake base, in dessert parfaits, or as a light snack on its own. It can be soaked with fruit or cream syrups, topped with frosting, jam, or fresh berries. For a more nutritious version, add nuts, dried fruit, or protein powder to the batter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep biscuit in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2–3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 1 week) or freeze (up to 2 months). Allow it to reach room temperature before serving to retain its soft texture.

cake-or-cupcake-white-no-icing.title: Cake or cupcake, white, no icing

content.title: About
content.content: This is a delicate white cake or cupcake without icing, made from a soft sponge batter. It has a light, airy texture and a mild buttery flavor, perfect for those who prefer simple desserts without sweet frosting.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White sponge cake is traditionally used as a base for many layered desserts.
The lack of icing makes this treat lower in sugar while preserving the rich taste of the batter.
The batter is often flavored with vanilla extract or lemon zest for added aroma.
Sponge cakes pair well with fruit fillings, creams, or fresh berries.
In some cultures a plain white cupcake is served with afternoon tea.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Sponge cake provides complex carbs that give sustained energy and satiety.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Without icing and with modest butter usage, it is less fatty than many other baked goods.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs in the batter supply a modest amount of high‑quality protein for tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and eggs contribute vitamins B1, B2 and B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The tender crumb is gentle on the stomach, making it suitable for sensitive digestion.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional sponge cake uses wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Eggs are a key ingredient; those allergic should avoid this product.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Even without icing, the batter usually contains sugar, so diabetics should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite lacking frosting, the cake still provides calories from flour, eggs, and sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the plain white cake or cupcake as a standalone dessert, slice into portions, or pair with berries, fruit sauce, or a light whipped cream. It also works well as a base for layered desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate – it will stay fresh for about a week. Bring to room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Plain butter crackers are dry baked snacks made from wheat flour, vegetable oil and a pinch of salt. They have a crisp texture, a subtle buttery flavor and are commonly eaten as a snack or as a base for sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crackers originated in Europe in the 19th century as a convenient way to preserve bread.
Traditionally they are made without added sugar, making them a neutral base for a variety of toppings.
In many countries they are served with cheese, pâté or vegetable dips.
Because the recipe uses vegetable oil, they are suitable for vegetarians but not vegans unless a plant‑based oil is used.
Crackers are often included in military rations due to their long shelf life.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Crackers provide quickly digestible carbs that can give an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: The absence of added sugar makes them suitable for people monitoring blood glucose levels.

items.title: Contain small amounts of B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour supplies B1, B2 and niacin, which support metabolism.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: Their neutral taste and crunch allow them to be combined with protein‑rich foods, enhancing overall nutrition when eaten as part of a balanced meal.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Crackers made from wheat flour can trigger reactions in individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because the carbs are rapidly absorbed, they may raise blood sugar levels, which is important for people with diabetes.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some varieties contain added salt, which should be limited by those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be enjoyed plain, spread with butter, cheese, hummus, avocado, or used as a base for canapés. They are also added to soups and salads for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For extended storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the oil from becoming rancid.

content.title: About
content.content: Crackers are thin, crunchy biscuits made from wheat flour, water, vegetable fats and a modest amount of salt. The reduced‑sodium version contains roughly half the salt of regular saltine crackers, making it a better choice for those monitoring sodium intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crackers originated in the United States in the early 19th century as a convenient way to preserve bread.
Reduced sodium is achieved by replacing part of the salt with flavor enhancers and spices.
Crackers are often used as a base for canapés and snack bites.
In some countries they are served with soup instead of bread.
Their light texture makes them easy to transport and store.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: The reduced salt level helps maintain normal blood pressure for individuals limiting sodium consumption.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat flour provides a slow‑release source of energy, contributing to prolonged satiety.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions are enriched with fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: Crackers pair well with low‑fat cheeses, hummus, or vegetable dips, allowing for a balanced snack.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat‑based crackers contain gluten and may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Some formulations include vegetable oils, so individuals watching fat intake should read the label.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: While most savory crackers are not sweet, a small amount of sugar is sometimes added for flavor balance.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, spread with low‑fat cream cheese, hummus, avocado, or used as a base for bite‑size canapés with vegetables and seafood.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store crackers in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep the bag tightly closed to retain crispness and prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit juice blend is a 100 % natural juice made from a mix of apples, pears, oranges and berries. The juice contains no added sugar, preservatives or artificial flavors. It offers a bright fruit taste and is rich in B‑vitamins, vitamin C and antioxidants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The juice is produced by cold‑press extraction, preserving most of the nutrients.
The fruit blend is selected to achieve an optimal balance of sweetness and acidity.
Demand for 100 % juices grew by more than 15 % in Russia during the 2020s.
The juice can be used as a base for smoothies, cocktails and marinades.
Packaging is made from recyclable PET, reducing the product’s carbon footprint.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: 100 ml of juice provides about 45 kcal, making it a light snack option.

items.title: Source of flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids from berries and citrus have anti‑inflammatory and antioxidant effects.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The juice is mostly water, helping to maintain the body’s hydration status.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to oranges or other citrus fruits in the blend.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although no sugar is added, natural fruit sugars can raise blood glucose levels in people with diabetes.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or reflux.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drink the juice chilled, use it as a base for smoothies, cocktails, fruit salads, or in cooking recipes as a water substitute.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 2‑6 °C. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Do not keep above 10 °C to prevent spoilage.

summer-squash-yellow-or-green-frozen-coo.title: Summer squash, yellow or green, frozen, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash (yellow or green) are young fruits of the zucchini plant that are flash‑frozen after harvest to retain freshness, flavor, and nutrients. Cooking them with butter or margarine adds a gentle richness and improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash belongs to the Cucurbitaceae family and is closely related to zucchini and other gourds.
Freezing within hours of picking preserves over 90 % of vitamin C.
Yellow and green varieties differ only in skin colour; their taste is virtually identical.
They are a staple in many Asian stir‑fry and braising dishes.
Cooking with butter or margarine increases the bioavailability of carotenoids.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Carotenoids that convert to vitamin A support vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a strong antioxidant and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Summer squash is low in calories and fat, making it suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Cucurbit allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to cucurbit vegetables.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Summer squash contains oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Added fat from cooking
items.content: Using large amounts of butter or margarine can make the dish calorie‑dense.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Quickly sauté the frozen squash in butter or margarine, add it to stews, soups, or serve as a side dish. It pairs well with garlic, fresh herbs (parsley, dill), and light sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen squash in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, use within 1–2 days and do not refreeze.
